analysis.one_liner: Bans states from requiring handguns to have loaded-chamber indicators, safeties that prevent firing, or shell-case markings.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in September 2024, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop federal, state, and local governments from enforcing any law requiring a handgun to have a device showing whether it is loaded, a mechanism that keeps it from firing unless the magazine is fully inserted, or the ability to stamp the gun's identifying information onto spent shell casings. It would also block any requirement for technologies designed to do those things or that could be converted to do them [S2]. The effect would be to void state-level handgun safety rules, such as California's microstamping and safety-feature requirements, and to prevent new ones [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Handgun manufacturers gain the most: they would no longer face state safety-feature mandates that require redesigning pistols for markets like California, avoiding engineering and retooling costs. Some gun buyers might see lower prices or more model choices in states that currently impose these requirements.

how_it_helps.text: The bill writes into federal law a prohibition on any federal, state, or local requirement that handguns include loaded-chamber indicators, magazine-disconnect safeties, microstamping capability, or technologies that perform or could be converted to perform those functions [S2].

Because federal law would override state rules, manufacturers would not have to build different versions of the same handgun for different states, sparing them the cost of redesigning or dropping models in states with safety mandates [S2].

analysis.who_pays: People shot unintentionally lose the protection of loaded-chamber indicators and magazine safeties, features designed to prevent accidental discharges. Police and prosecutors lose microstamping, a tool that can link spent shell casings found at crime scenes to specific guns. States that adopted these rules would see them nullified.
analysis.who_pays_short: Unintentional-shooting victims and state safety laws

drawbacks.text: The bill would override state safety rules that some states adopted after decades of work, nullifying loaded-chamber indicator, magazine-safety, and microstamping requirements in those states [S2].

If states can no longer require these features, manufacturers have little market incentive to add them voluntarily, since the features add per-unit cost; the safety features would likely disappear from guns sold nationwide, not just in states that required them.

Supporters would argue that some mandates, notably California's microstamping requirement, are technically impractical and have effectively kept new handgun models off that state's market, raising costs for lawful buyers without proven crime-fighting benefit. That is the strongest good-faith case for the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is concentrated: manufacturers avoid the cost of complying with state safety mandates, and buyers in restrictive states may see lower prices and more choices. The cost is diffuse but real: fewer safety features on the guns Americans actually handle, weaker investigative tools for police, and the invalidation of rules individual states chose for themselves. The name 'Modern Firearm Safety Act' points in the opposite direction from the bill's effect.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 2024 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never scheduled a hearing or vote, and the bill expired when the Congress ended in January 2025 [S4].

narrative.text: Senator James Risch of Idaho introduced the bill on September 25, 2024, with 12 other Republican senators as original cosponsors [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; that was the only action it ever received [S4].
Thirteen Republican senators total signed on as cosponsors, all from the Senate's Republican conference [S3].
No hearing, markup, or vote followed, and the bill died at the end of the 118th Congress in January 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the handgun safety rules states like California adopted remain on the books and enforceable, so residents of those states keep the loaded-chamber, magazine-safety, and microstamping protections the bill would have erased. Firearm manufacturers did not get the federal override they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States that kept their handgun safety rules

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or committee vote; the record shows no committee action after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 senators behind the bill were Republicans; no Democrat or independent cosponsored, and the Democratic-chaired Judiciary Committee took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would have barred any government from requiring loaded-chamber indicators, magazine-disconnect safeties, or microstamping, freeing manufacturers from state mandates that force design changes and per-unit safety costs [S2]. The industry's interest in avoiding those costs runs against the safety of the people who handle the guns, and federal preemption would have removed the states' power to require the features even if consumers wanted them.
